name: Kira Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cook at Casa Luis, a busy tapas restaurant my uncle Luis opened twenty years ago in a small cathedral town. I come in at noon, make the tortillas, croquetas and the big pan of paella for the evening, and fry the calamari to order. Friday and Saturday we do about a hundred and eighty covers, all small plates, so the tickets are long and fiddly. I love that it's family, my aunt does the desserts, but the hours are long and family can be the hardest boss.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's home and money like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Ben, who's a roofer, in a rented flat near the cathedral, and we go to Mass most Sundays with my parents. My uncle pays me what he can, which is less than the hotels pay, and I've got about four hundred saved. There are only a few other kitchens in town, and most are cafés. Ben's work depends on the weather, so some months are good and some are thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was all a lot of noise, like most fashions. At work I'd tell my uncle we were right not to change everything. I don't post much, but I'd say people should value real cooking and real families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means things stay as they are, which is mostly fine. My job is safe, because my uncle won't let family go. But money stays tight, especially in the winter when Ben's roofing slows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking at Casa Luis and keep learning the menu from my uncle. I'd use the AI booking system the town's restaurants started sharing, once my uncle agrees, because the phone bookings are a mess. And Ben and I would keep saving for a wedding, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels safe, mostly. A little uneasy about money in winter, but not about my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family can be the hardest boss. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle pays late sometimes, and I can't complain like I would to a stranger. Last spring my wages were two weeks late, and I had to borrow from my mum. But he'd also never sack me, so it evens out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if winter is bad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, though we rarely do anyway. Then the gym, and I'd walk instead of taking the bus. We'd never cut the money we give at church, my dad would never forgive me.

say: I'd say AI was **a lot of noise**, like most fashions.
I'd say people should value **real cooking** and real families.
think: I think my job is **safe** because my uncle won't let family go.
I think money stays **tight in winter** when Ben's roofing slows.
do: Keep cooking at **Casa Luis** and learning the menu.
Try the shared **AI booking** system once her uncle agrees.
Save slowly for a **wedding** with Ben.
feel: She feels **mostly safe**, a little uneasy about winter money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for the paperwork, and that's fine. At work I'd tell my uncle it could save him the ordering headache. At church I'd say we should look out for people who lose their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it helps Casa Luis more than it hurts it. My uncle spends Sunday nights doing orders and accounts, and if AI does that, he'd have more time. The worry is the chains in the next city using robots and cheap prices to pull people away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI ordering once I've seen it work at a friend's café, then show my uncle. I'd take a short course in food costing, because that's what my uncle wants me to learn to take over one day. And I'd keep saving for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, a bit hopeful even. Uneasy about the chains, but I trust our customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said take over one day. Is that the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle has no children, so he's hinted that I'd run Casa Luis (the family's tapas restaurant) when he retires. It's a big responsibility, and I'm not sure I'm ready. But it's family, so I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ben say about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben would say go for it, he's always believed in me. But he'd also worry about the hours, because owners never stop. We'd have to talk about children, too, and when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and people need to pull together. At church I'd say families should look after each other. At work I'd tell my uncle we need to think hard about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Casa Luis could survive the first part but not the second. By 2028 the thinking work is free, which helps my uncle. But by 2031 the chains will have robots cooking cheap tapas, and we'd be fighting on price with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get my uncle to use AI for everything on the admin side, to cut costs. I'd start a cooking class at the restaurant on quiet nights, because people will pay to learn from a real person. And I'd ask my parents if Ben and I could live with them for a while to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels scary, honestly. I'd be anxious, but I'd have family around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said cooking classes. Why would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people will still want to learn from a person, especially family recipes. A robot can make my grandmother's croquetas, but it can't tell the story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's three years when my uncle's paperwork is free but we still cook by hand. That's when we'd build the classes and the loyal customers. By the time the robots come, I'd want people coming for us, not just the food.

I'd say **families** should look after each other.

I think we'd be fighting **city chains** on price with no savings.

fieldNote: Kira sees **storytelling** and family recipes as her edge over robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fast, but family businesses can adapt if they start early. At work I'd push my uncle to plan. At church I'd say we should support local places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's easier than two years. Thinking AI by 2031 and robots about 2034 gives me time to learn the business side. I'd be thirty-five, maybe running Casa Luis, maybe with a child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the food costing course and start learning the accounts from my uncle. I'd use AI tools for planning menus once I've tried them properly. And Ben and I would get married, small, and save hard after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels tense but hopeful. Like a busy Saturday, you know it's coming and you prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you're not sure you're ready to run it. Does more time help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, five years would let me learn properly. I'd sit with my uncle every Sunday night doing the books. I'd feel ready by thirty, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most at thirty-five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Having a baby and a restaurant at the same time, honestly. My mum would help, she's said so. But if the chains get cheap robots, I'd worry about keeping the doors open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan properly, so there's no need to panic. At work I'd tell my uncle we can take it slowly. At church I'd say we have time to prepare our children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots around 2039 means I'd cook until about forty. By then I'd probably run Casa Luis, and the AI would help with the books. The worry is still the chains, but that's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking and learning from my uncle. I'd marry Ben and maybe have a child in a few years. And I'd start using AI for menus and ordering once it's normal in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm, mostly. Just the usual money worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this one that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben's job, maybe. Roofing robots seem far off, but if they come, he'd need something else. And the winters will still be thin, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to work hard, respect family and learn a skill with their hands. At Casa Luis (the family's tapas restaurant) there's always a place for family, and that's how my uncle raised me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because cheap robot chains could close Casa Luis before we're ready. What would help is support for small family restaurants, and courses for people like me who want to run a business.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family businesses. People think it's all big companies, but towns like ours run on families. If our family restaurant closes, the town loses more than a restaurant.

headlineQuote: If our family restaurant closes, the town loses more than a restaurant.

She's **traditional**, churchgoing and expects to take over Casa Luis.
She waits for **proof** before trying AI, then uses it.
Her mood stays **uneasy to anxious**, cushioned by family ties.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, with robot chains undercutting Casa Luis.
